system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2167-03-20 22:23:00 to 2167-03-22 13:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of Addison’s disease was admitted for fatigue, weakness, and lethargy following recent hand surgery and an active flare of microscopic colitis. She had been consuming minimal nutrition, mostly broth, and presented with symptoms concerning for adrenal insufficiency. Initial labs showed mild hyponatremia and elevated creatinine, consistent with dehydration. She received IV fluids overnight, which improved her kidney function and clinical status. Her symptoms resolved, and she was not in adrenal crisis. She was discharged the following day with temporary doubling of fludrocortisone and prednisone for three days, new prescriptions for calcium citrate and vitamin D, and instructions to hold metoprolol until steroid tapering was complete. Follow-up was arranged with endocrinology to reassess electrolytes and medication dosing.
problems: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re here because you’ve been feeling weak and had some abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been feeling really tired and weak for about a week. My dog passed away recently, and I’ve just been overwhelmed. I think I fell behind on my medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry to hear about your dog. That’s really tough. Which medications do you think you missed or adjusted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My prednisone and fludrocortisone for Addison’s. I usually adjust them when I’m stressed, but I didn’t keep up. I also felt nauseous and had loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When your body is under stress, you need more steroids, not less. Missing doses or not increasing them can lead to adrenal insufficiency, which explains your weakness and stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it could get this bad so quickly. In the ER, they gave me something in my IV—felt better fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you got hydrocortisone IV, which helps replace what your body was missing. That’s why you’re feeling better now. We also checked your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium was low at 133, and potassium was a bit high. That’s common in adrenal insufficiency. Your kidney function was slightly off too, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not treated, but you’re responding well. We’ll keep you on IV fluids tonight and start oral steroids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just glad I’m not as nauseous anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still a little tired, but my stomach feels fine. I’m really thirsty though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body is rehydrating. We’ll keep the IV going overnight to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your labs from this morning. Your sodium is up to 137, and potassium is normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means the treatment is working. We’ll switch you to oral prednisone today—20 mg this evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking 5 mg before. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is a temporary increase to help your body recover from the stress. You’ll taper it down over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I taper it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take 20 mg today and tomorrow, then 10 mg for two days, then back to 5 mg. We’ll write that down for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my fludrocortisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were taking it once daily, but we’re restarting it twice daily—0.1 mg in the morning and evening. That helps balance your sodium and potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Should I restart my blood pressure meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but only if your blood pressure is elevated. You can take amlodipine or metoprolol as needed. We’ll monitor it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endocrinology team stopped by. They agree with our plan and want you to follow up with them the day after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been managing this on my own for years, but I think I need more support, especially with everything going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Grief can really impact your health, especially with a condition like Addison’s. We can also connect you with counseling if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That might help. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look great. Kidney function is normal, and your electrolytes are stable. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to feel this good. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I ask about my other meds? I take omeprazole, Synthroid, and alendronate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking Synthroid in the morning. Omeprazole is now 20 mg twice a day—was it 40 mg before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 40 mg twice a day. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered it because high-dose PPIs long-term can affect bone health, and you’re on alendronate for osteoporosis. 20 mg twice a day is still effective for your reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And alendronate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking it weekly. Just remember to take it on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and stay upright for 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary with all the medication changes and follow-up instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. So, prednisone 20 mg today and tomorrow, then down to 10 mg, then 5 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And fludrocortisone twice daily. Call us if you feel weak, dizzy, or nauseous again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my endocrine appointment tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, first thing in the morning. They’ll check your labs and make sure everything’s on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in. I just need to stay on top of my meds and take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. And don’t hesitate to reach out if you’re struggling—medically or emotionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—can I travel next week? I was supposed to visit my sister.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should be fine, but carry your steroid card and a dose of injectable hydrocortisone in case of emergency. And don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always do. I learned that the hard way years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Just take it slow for the next few days. You’ve been through a lot, even if it was brief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m packing up now. I’ll make sure to take my meds on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll call you tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged. Take care, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to confirm—I take the 20 mg prednisone tonight, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tonight and tomorrow night. Then start the taper. We sent it to your pharmacy with clear instructions.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of Addison’s disease was admitted for weakness, abdominal pain, and malaise following the recent loss of her dog, which led to missed medication adjustments. She presented with hyponatremia and relative hyperkalemia, consistent with adrenal insufficiency. In the emergency department, she received IV hydrocortisone and fluids, with rapid improvement in symptoms. She was transitioned to oral prednisone with a tapering plan and restarted fludrocortisone twice daily. Labs normalized during her stay, and she remained stable. She was discharged home with medication adjustments, clear instructions for steroid tapering, and a scheduled follow-up with endocrinology the next day.
